what_it_does: Fuzzing is a security technique where you automatically generate thousands of slightly garbled inputs and feed them to a program to see if any cause it to crash or misbehave — revealing hidden bugs. Fuzzing an operating system kernel (the core software that manages all hardware and runs every other program) is especially valuable because kernel bugs can give attackers full control of a machine. The challenge is that kernel code is extremely complex: getting a test input to reach a specific deep code path requires a precise sequence of system calls (requests an application makes to the OS) with just the right arguments. Existing fuzzers mutate test programs using simple random guessing or hand-written rules, which rarely produce inputs that reach difficult code paths. Snowplow trains a machine-learning model on the kernel's actual source code — its call graphs and data flows — so the model learns which mutations (adding a system call, changing an argument value) are most likely to drive execution toward unexplored territory. The model's suggestions replace blind random guessing.
